questions.q: In this course, what does “2D-PAGE” refer to?
options: The standard protein gel electrophoresis that sorts proteins by size into a ladder.
The method that cuts proteins into fragments, weighs them and reads out their sequences.
Two-dimensional protein electrophoresis that separates first by charge and then by molecular weight.
The technique that weighs molecules and then identifies them from the patterns of the fragments they produce.
questions.why: 2D-PAGE is two-dimensional protein electrophoresis that separates first by charge using isoelectric focusing and then by molecular weight using SDS-PAGE; the ladder that sorts proteins by size is SDS-PAGE, while identifying molecules from their fragment patterns is the job of mass spectrometry.

questions.q: Every chemical reaction has to climb over an energy threshold, and an enzyme’s job is exactly to lower it — what is this concept called?
options: Activation energy
Active site
Substrate
Allostery
questions.why: Activation energy is the energy threshold a reaction has to overcome, which enzymes lower in order to speed the reaction up; Active site is the pocket where the reaction takes place, Substrate is the target that is acted upon, and Allostery is the effect of a molecule binding somewhere else and changing the shape and activity of the main site.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Active site” refer to?
options: Another molecule binds somewhere that is not the main site of action, yet changes the shape and activity of the main site.
The target on which the enzyme acts.
A protein that helps another protein fold correctly and stops them clumping together.
The groove on the enzyme into which the substrate fits just so, where the chemical reaction takes place.
questions.why: Active site is the groove where the enzyme binds the substrate and the chemical reaction actually happens; the thing that changes the shape of the main site is allostery, the target the enzyme acts on is the substrate, and the protein that helps with folding is the chaperone.

questions.q: Another molecule binds to the enzyme somewhere that is not the main site of action, yet changes the shape and activity of the main site — what is this phenomenon called?
options: The groove on the enzyme into which the substrate fits just so, where the chemical reaction takes place.
Besides the main site of action there are regulatory sites, and a molecule binding there can change the shape and activity of the main site.
The energy threshold every chemical reaction has to climb over, which enzymes lower.
A protein that helps another protein fold correctly and stops them clumping together.
questions.why: This is allostery: the regulatory molecule binds somewhere other than the main site of action and indirectly changes the shape and activity of the main site; Active site is the groove where the reaction actually happens, Activation energy is the threshold a reaction has to cross, and Chaperone is the protein that helps other proteins fold.

questions.q: What does “Alpha helix (alpha-helix)” refer to?
options: A shape in which several stretched-out protein chains lie side by side, held in place by hydrogen bonds between them.
The regular local shapes of a chain: alpha-helix and beta-sheet.
The corkscrew shape commonly adopted by protein chains, held up by hydrogen bonds between neighbouring turns.
The process by which a chain of amino acids twists into a specific three-dimensional shape so that it can do its job.
questions.why: Alpha helix is the corkscrew shape held up by hydrogen bonds between neighbouring turns; chains lying side by side and held by hydrogen bonds between them form a beta sheet, the two together are secondary structure, and a fold is the process of twisting the whole chain into a three-dimensional shape.

questions.q: The twenty small molecules that make up proteins, each carrying a variable side chain that decides how it folds — what are these small molecules called?
options: Amino acid
Peptide
Polypeptide
Peptide bond
questions.why: Amino acid is the building block of proteins: there are twenty of them, all sharing the same backbone and differing only in their R-group; a short chain is a peptide, a long chain is a polypeptide, and the bond that links amino acids together is the peptide bond.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Angstrom” refer to?
options: The smallest part of an antibody, variable region only. About 25 kDa.
The energy threshold every chemical reaction has to climb over, which enzymes lower.
Two-dimensional protein electrophoresis that separates first by charge and then by molecular weight.
The unit for measuring atomic distances; a crystal structure at 2.8 Å counts as good, and below 2.0 Å counts as excellent.
questions.why: Angstrom (Å) is the unit used to measure atomic distances; he said a crystal structure at 2.8 Å counts as good and below 2.0 Å counts as excellent. The 25 kDa of an Fv is a molecular mass, Activation energy is an energy threshold, and 2D-PAGE is an electrophoresis method for separating proteins — none of them is a unit of length.

questions.q: A Y-shaped protein made by B cells that recognises a single antigen, then blocks it or tags it so that it can be cleared away — what is this?
options: Antigen
Antibody
Epitope
Isotype
questions.why: Antibody is the Y-shaped protein made by B cells that recognises one antigen; the whole thing judged to be foreign is the antigen, the small patch the antibody actually touches is the epitope, and versions such as IgG1 and IgG4 are the antibody classes (isotypes).

questions.q: What is “Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC)”?
options: A Y-shaped protein made by B cells that recognises a single antigen, then blocks it or tags it so that it can be cleared away.
The three hypervariable loops in the variable region of an antibody, which together form the antigen-binding site.
The Fc portion of an antibody grabs an NK cell and orders it to kill the cell the antibody is stuck to.
An immune cell that can kill tumour cells without being given a target.
questions.why: In ADCC the Fc portion of the antibody grabs an NK cell and orders it to kill the target cell the antibody is stuck to; the Y-shaped protein itself is the antibody, CDR1–CDR3 form the antigen-binding site, and the NK cell is the immune cell that does the killing.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Antigen” refer to?
options: Something the immune system identifies as foreign and prepares to deal with.
The small patch on the antigen that the antibody actually touches.
The stem of the antibody — the part that recruits other parts of the immune system.
One version of an antibody class.
questions.why: Antigen is something the immune system identifies as foreign and prepares to deal with; the small patch the antibody actually touches is the epitope, the stem of the antibody is the Fc fragment, and the class of antibody is the isotype.

questions.q: Which amino acid is positively charged and basic, and appears on his slides in the group with bulky, charged R-groups?
options: Glycine
cysteine
Amino acid
arginine
questions.why: Arginine is a positively charged basic amino acid whose R-group is bulky and charged; Glycine has the smallest and most flexible side chain, while Cysteine carries a thiol that lets it lock onto another cysteine through a disulfide bond.

questions.q: A protein chain has two common regular local shapes: one is the corkscrew, and the other is several stretched-out chains lying side by side, held in place by hydrogen bonds between them. The latter is called ______.
options: Alpha helix
Beta sheet
Secondary structure
Tertiary structure
questions.why: The shape in which chains lie side by side, held by hydrogen bonds between them, is the beta sheet; the corkscrew is the alpha helix, the two together are secondary structure, and tertiary structure is the three-dimensional shape of the whole folded chain.

questions.q: A protein chain is always written from the N-terminus to the C-terminus; the amino acid at the far end of the chain carries a free carboxyl group, and this end is called ______.
options: N-terminus
N-terminal signal peptide
C-terminus
N-terminal domain (NTD)
questions.why: The end of a protein chain that keeps a free carboxyl group is the C-terminus; the end with the free amino group is the N-terminus, the N-terminal signal peptide is the address label that directs a protein to the endoplasmic reticulum, and the N-terminal domain is the regulatory region at the start of a nuclear receptor.

questions.q: Those three hypervariable loops in the variable region of an antibody that actually touch the antigen, which together form the antigen-binding site — what are they?
options: CDR1, CDR2 and CDR3
Variable region
VH
VL
questions.why: CDR1, CDR2 and CDR3 are the three hypervariable loops in the variable region of an antibody, and together they form the antigen-binding site; Variable region is the tip of the antibody arms that differs from antibody to antibody, and VH and VL are the variable regions of the heavy chain and the light chain respectively.

questions.q: What does “Chaperone” do?
options: The hard, insoluble lumps formed by misfolded proteins. They appear when recombinant proteins are made too fast or too early.
The process by which a chain of amino acids twists into a specific three-dimensional shape so that it can do its job.
The way several individually folded chains come together to form one working whole.
A protein that helps another protein fold correctly and stops them clumping together.
questions.why: Chaperone helps another protein fold correctly and prevents clumping; the hard, insoluble lumps built up by misfolding are inclusion bodies, twisting the whole chain into a specific shape is a fold, and several chains coming together into a working whole is quaternary structure.

questions.q: The small units on mRNA made of three letters, each specifying one amino acid — what are they called?
options: Nucleotide
Codon
Peptide
R-group (side chain)
questions.why: A codon is three letters on mRNA specifying one amino acid; a nucleotide is the base + sugar + phosphate building block of DNA and RNA, a peptide is a short chain of amino acids joined together, and the R-group is the side chain of an amino acid.

questions.q: What is special about the side chain of “cysteine”?
options: The amino acid with the smallest side chain, and the most flexible one.
A positively charged, basic amino acid.
The amino acid that carries a thiol, so two cysteines can be locked together by a disulfide bond.
The twenty small molecules that make up proteins, each carrying a side chain that decides how it folds.
questions.why: The side chain of Cysteine carries a thiol, and two cysteines can form a disulfide bond that locks the fold in place; the one with the smallest and most flexible side chain is glycine, and the positively charged basic amino acid is arginine.

questions.q: Left standing for a while, the amide beside asparagine in a protein spontaneously loses its amino group, passes through a succinimide intermediate and becomes aspartic acid or iso-aspartic acid. What is the most direct clinical meaning of this chemical change?
options: The storage conditions and shelf life of a therapeutic protein have to be tightly specified, and the proportion of iso-Asp may have to be checked.
The protein becomes more stable, so its shelf life can be extended.
The protein automatically reverts to its original correct amino acid sequence, with its structure completely unaffected.
The protein is broken down into amino acids and a new protein is synthesised afresh.
questions.why: Deamidation is the slow chemical change in which asparagine in a protein becomes aspartate, and it alters the potency of the protein; iso-Asp has the same mass as true Asp but a different bonding arrangement, which affects folding and binding, and that is why the storage conditions and shelf life of therapeutic proteins are tightly specified.

questions.q: A covalent link can form between the thiol groups of two cysteines, like a nail that pins the fold shut; this link is called ______.
options: Peptide bond
Tertiary structure
Protein domain
Disulfide bond
questions.why: The covalent link between two cysteines is the disulfide bond, and it helps hold the shape of the protein; the peptide bond is the link that joins an amino acid to the next one, tertiary structure is the three-dimensional shape of the whole folded chain, and a protein domain is a stretch that can fold on its own to do one job.

questions.q: The highly conserved part of a nuclear receptor that recognises its own DNA word — what is it called?
options: Ligand-binding domain (LBD)
DNA-binding domain (DBD)
N-terminal domain (NTD)
Protein domain
questions.why: DNA-binding domain (DBD) is the part of a nuclear receptor that recognises the DNA word; LBD is the part that houses the hormone or drug and changes shape when it does so, and NTD is the regulatory region at the start of the nuclear receptor.

questions.q: What is “Edman degradation”?
options: The method that cuts proteins into fragments, weighs them and reads out their sequences.
The technique that weighs molecules and then identifies them from the patterns of the fragments they produce.
The standard protein sequencing method, reading off one amino acid at a time from the N-terminus.
Two-dimensional protein electrophoresis that separates first by charge and then by molecular weight.
questions.why: Edman degradation is the traditional sequencing method that reads the sequence one amino acid at a time from the N-terminus; cutting proteins up and identifying them is the division of labour between LC-MS/MS and mass spectrometry, and 2D-PAGE is an electrophoresis method that separates proteins by charge and molecular weight.

questions.q: After a new protein is made in the cell, which membrane network does it enter first to be folded, checked and glycosylated?
options: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
The DNA-binding domain (DBD) of a nuclear receptor
The shipping route made up of the Golgi apparatus and vesicles
The membrane protein sitting in the cell membrane
questions.why: Endoplasmic reticulum is the membrane network beside the nucleus where new proteins are made, folded, checked and glycosylated; the Golgi apparatus and vesicles are the shipping route that comes after the ER, DBD is the part of a nuclear receptor that recognises DNA, and a membrane protein sits in the cell membrane.

questions.q: In this course, what is the definition of “Enzyme”?
options: The target on which the enzyme acts.
The groove on the enzyme into which the substrate fits just so, where the chemical reaction takes place.
The energy threshold every chemical reaction has to climb over, which enzymes lower.
A protein that speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed itself.
questions.why: An enzyme is a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction without itself being consumed in the reaction; the target the enzyme acts on is the substrate, the groove where the reaction happens is the active site, and the energy threshold that enzymes lower is the activation energy.

questions.q: When the CDR1–CDR3 of an antibody bind an antigen, what is the small patch on the antigen that is actually touched called, and how is it related to the antigen?
options: Antigen; it is the whole foreign object, of which the epitope is only one part.
Epitope; it is a small patch of the antigen, and it is the true target the antibody recognises.
Variable region; it is the tip of the antibody arms that differs from antibody to antibody.
Fab fragment; it is the one arm the antibody uses to grab the antigen.
questions.why: An epitope is the small patch of the antigen that the antibody actually touches; the whole thing judged to be foreign is the antigen, the part at the tip of the antibody arms that differs from antibody to antibody is the variable region, and the arm that grips the antigen is the Fab fragment.

questions.q: What role does “Fab fragment” play in antibody structure?
options: The stem of the antibody — the part that recruits other parts of the immune system.
The smallest part of an antibody, variable region only. About 25 kDa.
The arm of the antibody — the part that grabs the antigen.
The two longer chains of the antibody, forming the stem and part of the arms.
questions.why: The Fab fragment is the arm of the antibody and is responsible for grabbing the antigen; the stem that recruits other parts of the immune system is the Fc fragment, the smallest piece with only the variable region (about 25 kDa) is the Fv fragment, and the two longer chains are the heavy chain.

questions.q: The part of an antibody responsible for recruiting other parts of the immune system (for example holding on to an NK cell) — what is it called?
options: Fc fragment
Fab fragment
Fv fragment
Variable region
questions.why: The Fc fragment is the stem of the antibody, responsible for recruiting other parts of the immune system, and ADCC works by the Fc holding on to an NK cell; the arm is Fab, the smallest variable-region fragment is Fv, and the variable region is the part at the tip of the arms that differs from antibody to antibody.

questions.q: The process by which a chain of amino acids twists into a specific three-dimensional shape and can therefore do its job is called ______.
options: Misfolding
Protein domain
Inclusion body
Fold (protein folding)
questions.why: A fold is the process of twisting an amino acid chain into a specific three-dimensional shape; failing to fold into the correct shape is misfolding, a stretch that can fold on its own to do one job is a protein domain, and the hard, insoluble lumps formed by misfolding are inclusion bodies.

questions.q: What does “Fv fragment” refer to?
options: The arm of the antibody — the part that grabs the antigen.
The smallest part of an antibody, variable region only. About 25 kDa.
The stem of the antibody — the part that recruits other parts of the immune system.
The two shorter chains of the antibody, at the ends of the arms.
questions.why: The Fv fragment is the smallest fragment of an antibody, containing only the variable region, about 25 kDa; the arm is Fab, the stem is Fc, and the two shorter chains are the light chain.

questions.q: Which amino acid has the smallest side chain and is therefore the most flexible, the one that can fit into different folds most easily?
options: arginine
cysteine
Glycine
Amino acid
questions.why: Glycine has the smallest side chain and is therefore the most flexible; bulky, charged R-groups such as arginine make that stretch of chain rigid, and what makes cysteine special is that its thiol can form a disulfide bond.

questions.q: How is “Heavy chain” described in an antibody?
options: The two longer chains of the antibody, forming the stem and part of the arms.
The two shorter chains of the antibody, at the ends of the arms.
The variable region of the antibody heavy chain.
The variable region of the antibody light chain.
questions.why: The heavy chain is the two longer chains of the antibody, which make up the stem and part of the arms; the two shorter ones are the light chain, and the variable regions of the heavy chain and the light chain are called VH and VL respectively.

questions.q: Among the antibody classes, the difference between IgG4 and IgG1 directly changes therapeutic behaviour. Which of the following descriptions is correct?
options: IgG4 kills target cells by ADCC, and stays in the blood longer than IgG1.
IgG4 does not kill target cells by ADCC, and stays in the blood for a shorter time than IgG1.
IgG4 is exactly the same as IgG1: both kill targets by the Fc holding on to an NK cell.
IgG4 does not kill target cells by ADCC, and stays in the blood longer than IgG1.
questions.why: An isotype is one version of an antibody class: IgG1 kills by ADCC (the Fc holds on to an NK cell), whereas IgG4 does not, but it stays in the blood longer than IgG1 — that is exactly the difference he uses to contrast antibody design.

questions.q: When recombinant protein is made too fast or too early, misfolded protein clumps into hard, insoluble lumps; this product is called ______.
options: Protein domain
Inclusion body
Chaperone
Proteome
questions.why: Inclusion bodies are the hard, insoluble lumps formed by misfolded proteins; the protein that helps other proteins fold correctly and stops them clumping is the chaperone, a protein domain is a stretch that can fold independently, and the proteome is the whole set of proteins a cell makes at a given moment.

questions.q: What is one version of an antibody class called? He used the difference between IgG1 and IgG4 to make this point.
options: Epitope
Antigen
Isotype
Variable region
questions.why: Isotype is one version of an antibody class: IgG1 kills by ADCC, IgG4 does not. The small patch the antibody actually touches is the epitope, the whole thing judged to be foreign is the antigen, and the variable region is the part at the tip of the arms that differs from antibody to antibody.

questions.q: What does “LC-MS/MS” refer to in protein research?
options: The method that cuts proteins into fragments, weighs them and reads out their sequences.
The standard protein sequencing method, reading off one amino acid at a time from the N-terminus.
The technique that weighs molecules and then identifies them from the patterns of the fragments they produce.
The standard protein gel electrophoresis that sorts proteins by size into a ladder.
questions.why: LC-MS/MS is the modern method that cuts proteins into fragments, weighs them and reads out the sequence; the traditional method that reads one residue at a time from the N-terminus is Edman degradation, weighing molecules and identifying them from their fragment patterns is mass spectrometry, and sorting proteins into a ladder by size is SDS-PAGE.

questions.q: The part of a nuclear receptor that houses a hormone or a drug, and changes shape when it houses it — what is it called?
options: DNA-binding domain (DBD)
N-terminal domain (NTD)
Protein domain
Ligand-binding domain (LBD)
questions.why: Ligand-binding domain (LBD) is the part of a nuclear receptor that houses the hormone or drug and changes shape when it does so; DBD recognises the DNA word, and NTD is the regulatory region at the start of the nuclear receptor.

questions.q: How is “Light chain” described in antibody structure?
options: The two longer chains of the antibody, forming the stem and part of the arms.
The two shorter chains of the antibody, at the ends of the arms.
The variable region of the antibody light chain.
The smallest part of an antibody, variable region only. About 25 kDa.
questions.why: The light chain is the two shorter chains of the antibody, at the ends of the arms; the two longer ones are the heavy chain, and the variable region of the light chain is called VL.

questions.q: He set four protein research methods side by side: Edman gives the sequence, SDS-PAGE gives the size, X-ray crystallography gives the atomic shape. So for the pair mass spectrometry and LC-MS/MS, how is the work of separation and identification divided up?
options: The two are exactly the same, and LC-MS/MS is just the older name.
Mass spectrometry only sorts proteins by size into a ladder, while LC-MS/MS does the sequencing.
Mass spectrometry weighs molecules and identifies them from the patterns of their fragments; LC-MS/MS cuts proteins into fragments, weighs them and reads out the sequence.
Both require the protein to form a crystal before you can get any result.
questions.why: Mass spectrometry is the technique that weighs molecules and then identifies them from the patterns of the fragments they produce; LC-MS/MS cuts proteins into fragments, weighs them and reads out the sequence. Sorting by size is SDS-PAGE, atomic shape requires X-ray crystallography, and that method does need the protein to form a crystal.

questions.q: One class of proteins sits in the plasma membrane and is often a receptor; he singled out their value in drug development. Why?
options: Because drugs can reach them from outside the cell, they are excellent drug targets.
Because they turn ATP into ADP inside the cell, so blocking them cuts off the energy supply.
Because they can be isolated straight from blood for mass spectrometry, so they are the easiest to validate.
Because their amino acid sequence is the shortest, so they are the easiest to sequence by Edman degradation.
questions.why: Membrane proteins sit in the plasma membrane and are often receptors; drugs can reach them from outside the cell, which makes them excellent drug targets. Turning ATP into ADP is the job of a kinase, and sequencing by Edman degradation and identification by mass spectrometry are not their advantages.

questions.q: What does “Misfolding” refer to?
options: The hard, insoluble lumps formed by misfolded proteins. They appear when recombinant proteins are made too fast or too early.
A protein that helps another protein fold correctly and stops them clumping together.
The process by which a chain of amino acids twists into a specific three-dimensional shape so that it can do its job.
A protein that has not folded into the correct three-dimensional shape. This is one of the risks for therapeutic proteins.
questions.why: Misfolding is a protein that has not folded into the correct three-dimensional shape, and it is one of the risks for therapeutic proteins; the hard, insoluble lumps built up by misfolding are inclusion bodies, the protein that helps with folding is the chaperone, and the process of twisting into a specific three-dimensional shape is a fold.

questions.q: What is the formal name of the RNA copy that carries the instructions from DNA into the cytoplasm so that ribosomes make proteins accordingly?
options: Codon
mRNA (messenger RNA)
Peptide
Proteome
questions.why: mRNA (messenger RNA) is the photocopy of the recipe, sent from the nucleus to the factory floor; a codon is the three letters on mRNA that specify one amino acid, a peptide is the short chain of amino acids that is made, and the proteome is the whole set of proteins a cell makes at a given moment.

questions.q: What is the regulatory region at the start of a nuclear receptor called? It is completely different from a signal peptide, because it governs the receptor itself, not the transport of a protein.
options: N-terminal signal peptide
DNA-binding domain (DBD)
N-terminal domain (NTD)
Ligand-binding domain (LBD)
questions.why: N-terminal domain (NTD) is the regulatory region at the start of a nuclear receptor; the N-terminal signal peptide is the postal address that directs a protein to the endoplasmic reticulum, DBD recognises the DNA word, and LBD houses the hormone or drug.

questions.q: The short “mailing address” at the very front of a protein, which directs it to the endoplasmic reticulum and so into the secretory pathway, is called ______.
options: Signal peptide
N-terminal domain (NTD)
Post-translational modification
Membrane protein
questions.why: The short postal address at the front of a protein that directs it to the endoplasmic reticulum is the N-terminal signal peptide; the N-terminal domain is the regulatory region at the start of a nuclear receptor, post-translational modification is the chemical change added after the chain is made, and a membrane protein is a protein sitting in the cell membrane.

questions.q: What does “N-terminus” refer to?
options: The last end of a protein chain, where the amino acid carries a free carboxyl group.
The “address label” at the N-terminus of a protein, which sends it into the ER.
The regulatory region at the start of a nuclear receptor.
The first end of a protein chain, where the amino acid keeps a free amino group.
questions.why: The N-terminus is the first end of a protein chain, where a free amino group is kept; proteins are always written from the N-terminus to the C-terminus. The last end with the free carboxyl group is the C-terminus, and the address label that sends a protein into the ER is the signal peptide.

questions.q: How is “Natural killer cell (NK cell)” described?
options: The Fc portion of an antibody grabs an NK cell and orders it to kill the cell the antibody is stuck to.
An immune cell that can kill tumour cells without being given a target.
One version of an antibody class. IgG1 kills by ADCC; IgG4 does not.
Something the immune system identifies as foreign and prepares to deal with.
questions.why: A natural killer cell is an immune cell that can kill tumour cells without being given a target; the antibody’s Fc grabbing an NK cell and ordering it to kill is ADCC, and the class of antibody is the isotype.

questions.q: A short chain of amino acids joined together by peptide bonds is called ______.
options: Polypeptide
Protein domain
Peptide
Proteome
questions.why: A short chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds is a peptide; a long string of amino acids is a polypeptide, a stretch within a protein that can fold on its own is a protein domain, and the whole set of proteins a cell makes at a given moment is the proteome.

questions.q: The chemical bond on a protein chain that joins one amino acid to the next is called ______.
options: Peptide bond
Disulfide bond
Codon
Chaperone
questions.why: The chemical bond that joins one amino acid to the next is the peptide bond; a disulfide bond is the covalent link between two cysteines, a codon is the three letters on mRNA that specify an amino acid, and a chaperone is the protein that helps a protein fold.

questions.q: What does “Polypeptide” refer to?
options: A short chain of amino acids joined together by peptide bonds.
The process by which a chain of amino acids twists into a specific three-dimensional shape so that it can do its job.
A stretch inside a protein that folds on its own and does one job itself.
A long string of amino acids. Once it folds up, it is a protein.
questions.why: A polypeptide is a long string of amino acids, and once it folds up it is a protein; the short kind is a peptide, twisting into a specific three-dimensional shape is a fold, and a stretch that folds independently to do one job is a protein domain.

questions.q: The chemical change added to a protein chain after the chain has been made is called ______.
options: Primary structure
Post-translational modification
Proteome
Mass spectrometry
questions.why: The chemical change added after the chain is made is post-translational modification; primary structure is the amino acid sequence itself, the proteome is the whole set of proteins a cell makes at a given moment, and mass spectrometry is the technique that weighs molecules and identifies them from their fragments.

questions.q: What does “Primary structure” refer to?
options: The regular local shapes of a chain: alpha-helix and beta-sheet.
The three-dimensional shape of a whole polypeptide chain once it has folded up.
The amino acid sequence of a protein, read from one end to the other.
The way several individually folded chains come together to form one working whole.
questions.why: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence; the regular local shapes of the chain are secondary structure, the three-dimensional shape of the whole folded chain is tertiary structure, and several chains coming together into a working whole is quaternary structure.

questions.q: A stretch inside a protein that can fold on its own and does one job itself is called ______.
options: Protein domain
Subunit
Proteome
Inclusion body
questions.why: A stretch that folds independently and does one job is a protein domain; one of the chains in a protein made of several chains is a subunit, the whole set of proteins is the proteome, and the hard, insoluble lumps formed by misfolding are inclusion bodies.

questions.q: What is the whole set of proteins made by a cell or a tissue at a given moment called?
options: Polypeptide
Protein domain
Post-translational modification
Proteome
questions.why: The proteome is the whole set of proteins made by a cell or a tissue at a given moment; a polypeptide is a long string of amino acids, a protein domain is a stretch that folds on its own, and post-translational modification is the chemical change added after the chain is made.

questions.q: When he set out the four levels of protein structure, which level are haemoglobin and antibody examples of? What does that level mean?
options: The third level: tertiary structure, the three-dimensional shape of a whole polypeptide chain folded up.
The fourth level: quaternary structure, the way several individually folded chains come together to form one working whole.
The second level: secondary structure, the regular local shapes of the chain (alpha-helix and beta-sheet).
The first level: primary structure, the amino acid sequence itself.
questions.why: Haemoglobin and antibody are both machines made of several chains, so they belong to quaternary structure; primary structure is the sequence, secondary structure is the local shape of alpha-helix and beta-sheet, and tertiary structure is the three-dimensional shape of a single folded polypeptide chain.

questions.q: Amino acids share the same backbone (a central carbon carrying an amino group, a hydrogen and a carboxyl group), and only the variable side branch differs; this branch, which decides how the whole chain folds, is called ______.
options: Amino acid
Codon
R-group (side chain)
N-terminal domain (NTD)
questions.why: The variable side branch on an amino acid is the R-group (side chain), and it decides how the whole chain folds; an amino acid is the whole unit, a codon is the three letters on mRNA that specify an amino acid, and the N-terminal domain is the regulatory region at the start of a nuclear receptor.

questions.q: What does “SDS-PAGE” refer to?
options: The standard protein gel electrophoresis that sorts proteins by size into a ladder.
Two-dimensional protein electrophoresis that separates first by charge and then by molecular weight.
The method that resolves the precise three-dimensional atomic shape of a protein.
The technique that weighs molecules and then identifies them from the patterns of the fragments they produce.
questions.why: SDS-PAGE is the standard gel electrophoresis that sorts proteins by size into a ladder; 2D-PAGE is the two-dimensional electrophoresis that separates first by charge and then by molecular weight, atomic shape requires X-ray crystallography, and identifying molecules from their fragment patterns is mass spectrometry.

questions.q: What does “Secondary structure” refer to?
options: The amino acid sequence of a protein, read from one end to the other.
The three-dimensional shape of a whole polypeptide chain once it has folded up.
The way several individually folded chains come together to form one working whole.
The regular local shapes of a chain: alpha-helix and beta-sheet.
questions.why: Secondary structure is the regular local shape of the chain, that is alpha-helix and beta-sheet; the sequence itself is primary structure, the whole folded chain is tertiary structure, and several chains coming together into a working whole is quaternary structure.

questions.q: After a new protein is made in the rough ER, it travels through the Golgi apparatus, vesicles and the cell membrane to the outside of the cell; this shipping route is called ______.
options: N-terminal domain (NTD)
Secretory pathway
Protein domain
Proteome
questions.why: The route rough ER → Golgi apparatus → vesicles → cell membrane → outside the cell is the secretory pathway; the N-terminal domain is the regulatory region at the start of a nuclear receptor, a protein domain is a stretch that folds on its own, and the proteome is the whole set of proteins of a cell.

questions.q: If a protein lacks the “address label” at its N-terminus that sends it into the ER, it cannot enter the shipping route that starts at the rough ER. What is this address label called? ______.
options: Subunit
Membrane protein
Signal peptide
Chaperone
questions.why: The address label at the N-terminus of a protein that sends it into the ER is the signal peptide, the first key of the secretory pathway; a subunit is one chain of a multi-chain protein, a membrane protein is a protein sitting in the cell membrane, and a chaperone is the protein that helps a protein fold.

questions.q: What does “Substrate” refer to?
options: The target on which the enzyme acts.
The groove on the enzyme into which the substrate fits just so, where the chemical reaction takes place.
A protein that speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed itself.
The energy threshold every chemical reaction has to climb over, which enzymes lower.
questions.why: The substrate is the target on which the enzyme acts; the enzyme itself is the enzyme, the groove is the active site, and the energy threshold that enzymes lower is the activation energy.

questions.q: In a protein made up of several chains, what is any one of those chains called?
options: Protein domain
Proteome
Polypeptide
Subunit
questions.why: In a protein made of several chains, each one is a subunit; a protein domain is a stretch on the same chain that folds independently to do one job, the proteome is the whole set of proteins of a cell, and a polypeptide is a long string of amino acids.

questions.q: What does “Tertiary structure” refer to?
options: The amino acid sequence of a protein, read from one end to the other.
The three-dimensional shape of a whole polypeptide chain once it has folded up.
The regular local shapes of a chain: alpha-helix and beta-sheet.
The way several individually folded chains come together to form one working whole.
questions.why: Tertiary structure is the three-dimensional shape of a whole polypeptide chain once it has folded up; the sequence is primary structure, the regular local shapes are secondary structure, and several chains coming together into a working whole is quaternary structure.

questions.q: What does “Variable region” refer to?
options: The variable region of the antibody heavy chain.
The variable region of the antibody light chain.
The tip of the antibody’s Y-shaped arms, which differs from antibody to antibody and is responsible for grabbing the antigen.
The three hypervariable loops in the variable region of an antibody, which together form the antigen-binding site.
questions.why: The variable region is the tip of the antibody’s Y-shaped arms, which differs from antibody to antibody and grabs the antigen; the variable region of the heavy chain is VH, that of the light chain is VL, and what actually touches the antigen is CDR1, CDR2 and CDR3.

questions.q: What does “VH” refer to?
options: The variable region of the antibody heavy chain.
The variable region of the antibody light chain.
The tip of the antibody’s Y-shaped arms, which differs from antibody to antibody and is responsible for grabbing the antigen.
The three hypervariable loops in the variable region of an antibody, which together form the antigen-binding site.
questions.why: VH is the variable region of the antibody heavy chain, VL is that of the light chain, and it is the three CDRs between them that actually touch the antigen, while the whole tip is the variable region.

questions.q: The biomarker discovery pipeline he demonstrated himself found the protein by using 2D-PAGE to compare normal liver, cirrhosis and HCC samples of different sizes. What is that protein, and what is its clinical significance?
options: Vimentin; but it exists only inside cells, so it cannot be measured in serum.
Chaperone; it is a structural protein inside the cell and leaks into the blood in liver cancer.
Proteome; it is a structural protein inside the cell and leaks into the blood in liver cancer.
Vimentin; it is a structural protein inside the cell and leaks into the blood in liver cancer, so it can be measured in serum by ELISA.
questions.why: Vimentin is a structural protein inside the cell that is released into the blood in hepatocellular carcinoma; 2D-PAGE showed that it rises early, it was then validated with qPCR, IHC and Western blot, and finally measured in serum by ELISA. A chaperone is the protein that helps proteins fold, and the proteome is the whole set of proteins a cell makes at a given moment — neither of them is that serum marker.

questions.q: What is the formal abbreviation for the variable region of the antibody light chain?
options: VH
VL
Fc fragment
Fv fragment
questions.why: VL is the variable region of the antibody light chain; VH is that of the heavy chain, the Fc fragment is the stem of the antibody, and the Fv fragment is the smallest piece, containing only the variable region (VH plus VL).

questions.q: He set four protein research methods side by side: Edman gives the sequence, LC-MS/MS gives identity and amount, SDS-PAGE gives the size. So which method is used to resolve the precise three-dimensional atomic shape of a protein, and what is its limitation?
options: Edman degradation; the protein must form a crystal first, otherwise you cannot read off the amino acids one by one.
SDS-PAGE; as long as the protein is charged, you can read off the positions of the atoms by size.
X-ray crystallography; the protein has to form a crystal first, which is why a protein such as histone, with its large positive charge and extreme flexibility, is very hard to crystallise.
Mass spectrometry; the positions of every atom can be worked backwards from the patterns of the fragments.
questions.why: X-ray crystallography uses X-ray diffraction plus mathematical inversion to work out the position of every atom, but the molecule must be able to form a crystal, which is why histone, with its large positive charge and extreme flexibility, is so hard to crystallise; Edman degradation is sequencing, SDS-PAGE separates by size, and mass spectrometry weighs molecules and reads the fragments.
